schema.name: Interacting system
roles: one part
another part
conditions: the system has two or more parts
the parts interact with one another
something happens at the level of the whole
excludes: systems with only one part

schema.name: Differentiation sustained by relation
roles: entity A
entity B
the relation coupling them
conditions: COUPLING: each entity's course depends on the other's; a shared external cause acting separately on both does not count
MODIFICATION: the coupling changes what at least one entity actually becomes, compared with what it would be uncoupled
INVARIANCE: each entity remains individuable afterwards as the same kind of thing it was, and can still be picked out on its own
DIFFERENTIATION: the change makes the entities LESS alike, or each less like its own uncoupled counterpart; a change that makes them more alike fails this
ENSEMBLE ORDER: a regularity holds over the collection that no single entity carries, represents or decides
excludes: entities that merge, dissolve or fuse so that they can no longer be told apart or handled separately
entities that come to resemble one another more closely through the interaction, such as synchronising or levelling
entities that resemble one another through a common external cause without acting on each other
entities unaltered by the relation, having been made to fit beforehand
a single pair whose interaction produces nothing beyond that pair

conditions: exactly two distinct units exist within the system
the relationship between those two units is mutual rather than one-directional
each unit's state changes as a consequence of that relationship (it cannot be determined from its own internal conditions alone)
no stable, identifiable boundary exists at which the two units become fully separable while both persist
the system does not contain any larger collection or grouping of multiple such pairs
there is no single third party that governs, decides, or arbitrates the relationship between the two units
excludes: a system in which one unit influences the other but remains unaffected and fully self-contained (one-directional causation)
a system of more than two interacting units whose pairwise relationships can be decomposed into independent pairs
two units that interact only with each other's outputs while remaining entirely independent internally, such that each could in principle exist without the other and retain its full identity
a triad or larger group where a third element mediates, judges, or standardizes the relationship between two elements
schema.name: binary coupling with mutual dependence and no separability or external governance
roles: couple A
couple B

conditions: The relation is *irreversible without cost* — one party cannot exit and re-enter on its own terms; the whole relationship must be reconstructed from scratch if it breaks.
The relation produces *emergent capability* — some function or outcome exists only while they are coupled together, unavailable to either in isolation.
Each party's behaviour is *path-dependent on the other* — where each goes next depends minute-by-minute on what the other does right now; neither follows a fixed plan that ignores the partner.
excludes: The relation is *reversible without cost*: parties can detach and reattach freely, with no memory of prior encounters, so they are not truly coupled. (A relationship where each side remains fully free to go its own way and restart identically — like a handshake that leaves both hands unchanged — does NOT fit.)

The relation yields *only additive outcomes*: what the pair produces is just the sum of what each would produce alone, so no new capability emerges from their coupling. (A partnership whose combined output equals the simple addition of its parts does NOT fit.)

The relation can be *dissolved with no reconstruction cost* — one party simply leaves and resumes an independent course while the other remains whole and capable on its own. (This is a shared market or competitive arrangement between otherwise-free agents, which does NOT fit; here each keeps its own books, name, and standing.)

The relation's *spacing or configuration is fixed by an external authority*: a third body decides how far apart the parties must be and can move them at will. (A relationship governed from outside — where some committee sets the terms of separation and revises them arbitrarily — does NOT fit; here what holds between the two is determined only by their mutual arrangement.)
schema.name: Coupled-Continuant Relation
roles: Party A: a continuing entity that cannot independently reconstruct its shared state with B once they part.
Party B: a continuing entity that cannot independently reconstruct its shared state with A once they part.

conditions: The structure is a relation between two parts that co-exist within one larger whole; neither part qualifies as an independent instance of the type on its own.
There exists at least one boundary (spatial, informational, or functional) beyond which each part ceases to depend on the other for existence and may be removed.
There exists a region outside that boundary—another instance of the same type or a wider environment—so that both parts are embedded within something else rather than being terminal.
excludes: Two separate agents that merely interact (e.g., two firms pricing against each other) because each can persist without the other and neither is confined to a shared whole.

A hierarchy of three or more levels where one level both contains and is contained by another (e.g., a market containing firms, each firm containing workers), since containment runs in opposite directions rather than nesting one inside the other at a single level.

Two parts bound together with no separating boundary possible (e.g., root and fungus fused into a chimeric whole that cannot be split apart or grown independently), because there is no region where they are free.
schema.name: Nested Boundary
roles: a part contained within another instance of the same type
another instance of the same type (or wider environment) in which it is embedded

conditions: The system contains two distinct parts.
There is a reciprocal dependency: each part's behavior depends on the other.
excludes: Systems with only one part, even if that single part internally regulates itself.
Systems in which one part affects the other but not vice versa (one-directional influence).
Systems whose two parts are independent and each behaves identically regardless of the other's presence or state.
schema.name: Reciprocal Dependency
roles: Part A
Part B

conditions: There are at least two distinct entities in a shared system.
The entities interact and each one's behaviour depends on the other over time; an individual cannot be described without reference to its counterpart(s).
The mutual dependence is produced by their being together, not by some external mechanism that acts on each of them independently — so splitting the system apart destroys or changes the relationship.
The two entities stay recognisably different from one another; they do not merge into a single unit.
excludes: A collection of things held together only by an external rule or force that acts on each member separately — e.g., any group where the members could be pulled apart and each kept as it was, with nothing lost.
Two things whose similarity or coordination comes from being copied from a common origin (e.g., two trees grown from the same parent stock) rather than from interacting directly with one another.
schema.name: coupling
roles: a system of at least two distinct entities
each entity whose behaviour depends on the others over time

conditions: There exist two distinct elements in a system: an originator and a recipient.

The recipient's form is produced by following the originator's structure with no direct causal input from the originator itself; transmission travels through a rule, convention, or shared procedure rather than through a direct interaction between the two entities
Both elements arrive at the same configuration (or an equivalent one) via that rule without any of the recipient's state depending on the originator's current state
The originator is invariant with respect to the recipient; its state, output, or behaviour changes nothing about itself whether or not it has a recipient following it
Neither element acts upon the other in either direction; there is no feedback, signalling, or mutual influence between them (the relationship is strictly unidirectional and passive)
The likeness shared between them is fully determined by an external mechanism rather than by any inherent property of either element alone
excludes: Any system in which the recipient's state causally depends on signals, inputs, or outputs from the originator (i.e. a causal feedback loop) at all
Any system in which either element modifies its own structure because of knowledge that it is being imitated or copied by another
Any system whose resemblance arises from an internal shared property rather than from following an external rule or convention
schema.name: Rule-based structural mimicry without causal coupling
roles: originator: the entity that establishes a structure, form, procedure, or pattern

recipient: the entity that acquires the same structure by following the originator's rule through some shared medium (a rule, convention, standard, weighting scheme, environmental force, or spelling agreement)

conditions: "role1" moves.
schema.name: Independent-Parallel-Duplicate
roles: agentA
agentB

conditions: The system has at least one part that is a stable carrier of structure — an entity whose identity is fixed by form alone and that persists across interactions.
That structure is reproduced in the output as an exact copy or near-identical form, not merely echoed qualitatively.
The carrier's own state, composition, or trajectory remains unchanged (or changes only incidentally) by virtue of having been copied; it does not depend on or respond to its copies.
A single independent instance replicates the structure without reference to any other instance — remove all copies and each original stands in unaltered form.
The similarity among instances is a consequence of sharing a common template, not of mutual influence, signaling, feedback, or selection pressure between them.
No instance modifies another; there is no information flowing back from copy to carrier that would change the carrier's behavior or structure.
excludes: Systems in which copies are functionally interdependent — e.g., two components that must cooperate for either to operate.
Systems governed by feedback loops, where outputs loop back to alter inputs and thus shape subsequent instances.
Systems with evolutionary selection or adaptation, where variants are filtered by fitness and the population changes over time in response to environment.
Systems where the resemblance between members arises from convergent optimization or shared environmental pressure rather than from a copied template.
schema.name: template reproduction
roles: carrier: a stable entity that embodies a fixed form or structure
copy: an output that reproduces the carrier's form without altering it
template: the invariant from which copies are derived and by which they remain identical to the source

conditions: Roles are fixed and distinct: at least two named parts A and B exist structurally within the system.
A stable relation R holds between A and B (a coupling, dependency, or correspondence that persists across time).
The system produces a single emergent entity E — a figure, shape, form, practice name, or written token — whose identity is defined by that relation rather than by either part.
E does not act back on A or B: neither part changes its behavior in response to E's existence; E is passively constituted and then inert toward the parts it summarizes.

A and B remain autonomous with respect to each other: they do not signal, coordinate, or adapt to one another to maintain R. E exists because of their passive coexistence or stable coupling, not because of mutual causation.

The mapping from A/B into E is defined by an external convention (weighting, standard form, established spelling rule) rather than by the intrinsic nature of A or B; the relation encodes a stipulation that holds regardless of how the parts evolve independently.
excludes: Systems where part A directly causes change in part B — mutual causation (both act back on each other).
Systems where E has agency: feedback loops, regulation, or adaptation by E toward its source.
Intrinsic properties of a single self-contained component considered in isolation, with no relation to another named part.
Relations that are the product of active coordination or communication between parts.
schema.name: The Emergent Correspondence
roles: A
B
E

conditions: There are at least two distinct roles in the system.
Each role produces a stable feature of the whole that is independent of other roles.
excludes: A system where one role actively shapes another, so the resulting feature depends on their interaction.
schema.name: Independent parallel duplication
roles: Two or more independently reproducing elements within a shared whole.
The stable pattern each element contributes.

conditions: The parts are real constituents of the system (things that exist), and they keep their identity through interaction.
Each part changes its own traits in response to meeting other specific parts, but no change is imposed on another part by virtue of that encounter.
Every part stays recognizably what it was before; none loses its individuality or merges into a bigger unit.
Each part becomes narrower: its range over something (its options, targets, values) shrinks after the interaction.
The narrowing is driven by mutual constraint on that single dimension — proximity to other parts pushes each one toward an extreme of it.
A stable configuration results in which no remaining movement along that dimension reduces tension among the parts.
No central authority or external designer sets the resulting pattern; it emerges only from the pairwise interactions of the parts.
excludes: Systems where a leader, controller, or designer assigns roles and determines positions.
Systems where one part directly manipulates another (physical force or direct control) rather than merely constraining each other's choices.
Systems whose result is dominated by external factors instead of mutual interaction.
schema.name: Competing Narrowing
roles: Two or more self-maintaining parts
A single dimension of choice that constrains their interactions

conditions: The system decomposes into distinct agents, each internally whole and independently persistent.
Each agent's local environment is the aggregate effect of all other agents acting on it.
No single agent can predict or compute that collective aggregate; it exists only from outside.
excludes: A system where one part can fully compute the global outcome and steer itself to match.
A system whose whole is reducible to a sum of pre-existing, fixed parts with no emergent order.
A system governed by an external authority that assigns each agent its role.
schema.name: Emergent Structural Partition
roles: agents
local environment

conditions: There are at least two distinct kinds of actor in the system.
Each kind of actor has its own machinery that lets it reproduce on its own terms — so a change to one actor does not automatically produce a change in another.
The actors interact by sharing resources or signals rather than by inheriting changes from each other directly.
Actors respond only when something specific comes their way; nothing drives them simply for being present next to others.
When they act, the response is geared toward keeping their own function and their ability to reproduce on their own terms.
excludes: A system where one part literally carries another — that inherits changes wholesale cannot shrink its own repertoire by making a deal.
A system where every component acts as if it has no independent identity, so nothing needs to stay itself while it adapts.
A single actor reacting alone to an external force with no other kind of participant; the pattern needs two kinds of actor that each keep their own machinery.
schema.name: Adaptive Partition
roles: Actor kind A — one distinct type in the system.
Actor kind B — a second, distinct type in the system

conditions: The candidate consists of N distinct kinds of element (N >= 2), where a kind is defined by what it does and how it interacts, not by its label.

Each kind can operate as an isolated singleton: take any one kind alone in isolation and specify that it remains unchanged over time (no growth, no shrinking, no switching to another kind). Call this property 'self-stability'.

For at least one pair of kinds A and B that both exist simultaneously in the candidate, their interaction produces a state change: either they transform into new kinds, or they remain the same kinds but each is altered from its pre-interaction state. This transformation must occur to make room for another transformation.

There exists a specific kind C such that (a) C cannot self-stabilize as an isolated singleton — it transforms when alone — yet (b) C persists in some stable, untransformed form within the multi-kind configuration.
The set of kinds present is stable under the system's dynamics: no kind appears or disappears over time; only their arrangement shifts.
excludes: A single kind that transforms in isolation and produces a new kind by consuming itself (e.g., a cell dividing, a firm splitting — where each survivor is an identical copy of the original). Excluded because there is no second kind to transform into; only one kind exists.

Any system with fewer than two distinct kinds. For example: a population of identical agents competing, or a single entity that evolves into variants of itself but remains within its own kind — these have no second kind to balance the first's transformation.

A set where every pair transforms into an entirely different new kind (e.g., A becomes X and B becomes Y). Excluded because there is no C that survives; all kinds are consumed by every interaction, leaving nothing persistent to anchor a stable configuration.
schema.name: Balanced Transformation
roles: Kinds: the distinct types of element present (each defined by its behavior and interactions).
Transformations: irreversible state changes that occur between coexisting kinds.
Singletons: any kind considered as an isolated unit within the set.

conditions: there are at least two distinct roles present in the system
each role possesses some resource, property, capacity, or position that can be exchanged, modified, or reconfigured through interaction with another role
excludes: a single role acting alone without any other role to interact with
an equilibrium state where the roles' properties remain unchanged after interaction (no narrowing occurs)
schema.name: Complementary Narrowing under Coexistence
roles: Two or more distinct roles that engage in a recurring mutual interaction, each holding some exchangeable resource, property, position, or capacity
A shared environment or market into which these interacting roles collectively provide coverage of some demand space

conditions: the system contains at least two components that remain distinct entities over time; merging them into one unit is not how the outcome arises
each component retains its own identity, form, rules of reproduction or renewal, and internal machinery throughout
excludes: a single agent acting alone to optimise itself and reshape its surroundings at will; this pattern requires two parties that can neither fully control nor simply ignore each other
a centrally governed outcome produced by a planner or shared model of the whole system, because here no component represents the global result
schema.name: Emergent structural complementarity in a multi-part system with persistent distinct identities
roles: two or more components that remain recognisable and autonomous throughout (e.g., two entities with separate identity, form, reproduction, resources)
a shared environment each component is embedded in

conditions: The system decomposes into a plurality of self-contained agents; each is internally coherent and retains its own identity, machinery, goals, and ability to persist on its own terms.
Each agent's optimal standalone state (what it would do if alone) requires occupying a broader domain than the region actually available once all others are present.

Adjacent agents exert mutual pressure on one another: each adjusts its behavior toward another partly in response to that other's adjustments, and neither can complete this adjustment unilaterally without the other.

Each agent's adjustment narrows or specializes it relative to its standalone baseline (it gives up part of what it would otherwise do), yet keeps enough of itself that it remains recognizably the same kind of thing.

The adjustments are self-reinforcing and mutually consistent: each step of adjustment makes the other's corresponding step more necessary, so neither agent can hold its original broader position while all others have narrowed toward it.
No single agent (or any external coordinator) computes or represents the final arrangement; the pattern only exists once every agent has acted on all the others and settled.
excludes: Systems where agents interact but each keeps its full standalone range regardless of others' presence, so no pressure to narrow arises.
Systems with a central coordinator that computes positions for everyone (e.g., a planner, an auctioneer, or any authority), because the arrangement is then designed rather than emergent.
Systems where agents specialize only as a by-product of pursuing their own independent goals without mutual responsiveness, so no narrowing pressure exists between them.
Competitive systems in which each agent shrinks its scope purely to maximize its own outcome (profit, fitness) while leaving the other's scope unchanged and with no reciprocal adjustment.
schema.name: Complementary Partitioning
roles: A plurality of self-contained agents (each internally coherent)
The shared domain over which they compete
Mutual responsiveness between adjacent agents

conditions: There exist at least two distinct roles that relate to one another.
Each role has a distinct way of persisting and reproducing (i.e., it is stable in its own right).
The contact between the two roles produces an outcome each role does not intend but accepts.
excludes: Any system with only one role or no relationship between the roles.
A hierarchy where a higher unit controls, commands, or owns a lower unit (i.e., dominance without mutual exchange).
An internal whole/part composition where components are merely assembled (e.g., a machine built from parts).
schema.name: Cooperation under division of labor
roles: Two or more distinct roles, each with its own way of persisting and reproducing.
A relationship between these roles involving mutual exchange (e.g., resources, services, information).
An outcome that emerges from the interaction but is not intended by any role.

conditions: The system has at least two persisting roles that keep their own identity across time.
The interaction between the roles makes each role more specialised than it would be in isolation.
No single agent represents or plans the emergent outcome.
excludes: Systems where one party is destroyed or absorbed by the other, so no identity survives to persist.
Systems where the interaction yields a shared capability but leaves each role exactly as specialised as it would have been alone.
schema.name: emergent
roles: A1
B1

conditions: The system is composed of two or more entities that are each self-contained: individually they retain their own mechanisms for maintenance, replication, and identity.

Each entity's behaviour in the relationship is reactive rather than designed toward the other; nothing computes the resulting arrangement, sets it as a goal, draws the partition, or coordinates with others to produce it.

When two entities are brought into interaction (by proximity, by binding, by price and product positioning, by acoustic similarity), each makes local adjustments that narrow its own range of what it does in relation to the other: fewer specialised structures, a more limited line of offering, a narrower recognition scope, or greater separation from a confusable partner.
Each entity remains recognisably itself after this adjustment — it still uses its own machinery and keeps its original identity; the change is a constraint on expression, not a takeover by the other.

The resulting configuration covers the relevant space (the environment's resources, an antigenic repertoire, market demand, or acoustic contrast) in a partitioned arrangement, but no single entity represents that total coverage as belonging to it.

The pattern emerges across many such pairs and settles into a stable structure — a mosaic of gaps, a repertoire of clones, a division of demand, a spread-out inventory, or an allocation network — none of which any participant computes or plans.
excludes: A single entity that alone maintains everything the system needs; with no counterpart to react against there is nothing to adjust toward.

Any arrangement that some agent has deliberately designed, computed centrally, or coordinated among themselves as a plan — including a central controller laying out the layout and distributing roles to others.
Cooperation achieved by design in which each participant's action is aimed at a shared goal rather than being an incidental consequence of local responses.
schema.name: Emergent Relational Structure
roles: self-contained entity with its own machinery for identity and reproduction
interaction partner that provokes reactive adjustment in the first role's range of behaviour

conditions: The system contains at least two distinct entities (call them A and B) that are fundamentally different in kind.

Entity A gives entity B a resource that only A can produce, and entity B gives back to A a resource that only B can provide. The exchange is mutually beneficial: each keeps something it needs more than the other offers.
Each entity remains independent and self-sustaining after giving; neither becomes dependent on the other for its reproduction or existence.
Entity A responds to being paired with B by reducing its own independent capacity to acquire what it gives (its 'own way' of doing the same thing lessens), yet stays fully capable.
Entity B, in turn, narrows some part of its original repertoire—trading away a capability or range while retaining its core identity—and remains capable on its own terms.
The arrangement does not produce a single merged entity; both A and B keep their separate identities and reproduce independently.
Over time the specific pairings settle into a pattern where how entities are linked cannot be captured by looking only at any one member's local connections.
excludes: A system in which both parties become dependent on each other for reproduction, identity, or existence—where losing the partner means ceasing to function as that entity.
An exchange where neither party gives up part of its own independent capacity, so the pairing changes nothing about how either operates alone.
A system in which one party is consumed, destroyed, or permanently altered by the exchange rather than remaining itself after giving.
A single fused entity that emerges from and depends on two original parts—there is no 'both stay separate' because there is only the whole.
Purely competitive systems where parties gain at each other's expense through one party's decline, with no mutual benefit arising from pairing.
schema.name: Mutual partial-dependence
roles: A: an entity that produces a resource uniquely available to it and trades it away while remaining itself.
B: an entity that gains something only A can offer and gives back something only B can provide, narrowing part of its own repertoire while staying itself.

conditions: the exchange is mutual: each part gains something it lacks (A needs what B supplies; B needs what A supplies).
the exchange is continuous and self-sustaining, not a one-time transaction.
each part keeps its own identity and can persist/reproduce on its own terms — no part dissolves into the other to form a single new thing.
neither part gives up its whole repertoire in order to join: each retains capacity for what it does outside the exchange (its non-partner functions remain available).
each part's contributions are modulated by partnership, not erased: being joined changes how much of each capability is expressed, but does not remove the underlying capability.
the arrangement is emergent and distributed: it cannot be reduced to a single central controller or a fixed one-to-one pairing that fully accounts for who connects to whom.
no part is purely subordinate: both sides are active contributors (both give), so neither relation reads as simple exploitation.
excludes: a predator-prey relationship, where one gains at the other's expense and the exchange is not mutual.
an owner-employee or buyer-supplier transaction, where terms are fixed in advance by contract rather than emerging through ongoing reciprocal adjustment.
two parts fusing into a single new entity (merger), where neither retains its own separate identity.
a relationship of pure domination or parasitism, where one side gains without the other gaining anything in return.
schema.name: Mutual Symbiotic Network
roles: Part A: a self-sustaining entity that lacks something and can supply another thing.
Part B: a self-sustaining entity that lacks what A supplies and can supply what A needs.

conditions: The system contains at least two distinct parts (call them A and B) that each contribute something the other lacks.
Each part provides a resource or capability to the other: A supplies one thing it possesses, while B supplies a different thing it possesses, so both directions of exchange are real.

Receiving this foreign input causes each part to reduce some quantity it would otherwise produce on its own—A produces less of its normally-generated version of that very resource (the same category), and B does likewise for its own.
excludes: Systems where A's gain in efficiency means B simply stops or is bypassed, rather than both sides continuing to produce their native goods more poorly.
A partnership whose outcome is a single new entity, hybrid, or merged structure instead of two parts that persist unchanged in kind.
An exchange in which only one side gives and the other merely receives without reciprocating—there must be mutual contribution for both directions to exist.
schema.name: Mutual partial-optimization through cross-supply
roles: A: a part capable of producing at least one good or capability independently.
B: a second distinct part capable of producing a different good or capability independently.

conditions: The system has at least two distinct parts (roles), where each part is self-identifiable and retains a stable identity across the interaction.

Each part contributes something the other lacks or needs: there exists an asymmetry in which role A provides a resource/function that role B cannot obtain on its own, while role B provides a different resource/function that role A cannot obtain on its own.

The relationship is mutual and ongoing rather than one-way: each part receives more (a net gain) from the exchange than it gives up, such that neither party's presence makes the other strictly worse off.
The interaction produces a coupling or coordination between the parts: their behaviors, states, or outcomes become interdependent in some recognizable pattern.
Each part continues to operate according to its own internal principles and goals; participation is not equivalent to assimilation (neither part loses its identity).
excludes: Systems where one party only takes without giving back, or gives without receiving a distinct return.
schema.name: mutual-coupling
roles: a provider of X that lacks Y
a provider of Y that lacks X

conditions: Two or more distinct roles exist within the system.
Each role provides something that another role needs or values.
The exchange of goods/services between roles is mutual and ongoing, not one-directional.
At least one role reduces its own independent capacity as a result of participating in the relationship.
This reduction persists across multiple interaction cycles, indicating structural change rather than a temporary adjustment.
Each role retains its fundamental identity and can operate independently when removed from the relationship.
excludes: Systems where one party benefits without reciprocating or reducing their own capacity.
Temporary or transient interactions that do not lead to lasting structural change.
Relationships where roles are fully merged into a single entity with no independent operation possible.
Hierarchical structures where authority flows in one direction rather than through mutual exchange.
schema.name: Reciprocal Capacity Reduction
roles: A system consisting of two or more distinct functional roles that engage in sustained reciprocal exchange
Each role must provide value to another role while receiving complementary value in return

conditions: The system contains at least two distinct participants who retain their individual identity and reproduce independently; neither participant is absorbed into or replaced by the other.
Each participant provides a resource that the other values, and this provision arises from each participant's own capacity rather than being handed to the other free of cost.
The amount exchanged in each direction varies over time and depends on current circumstances: it is not a fixed quota written into either participant.

Participants adjust their supply based on what they receive — those who get more give more, those who get less give less; this adjustment happens at the point of contact between pairs rather than from one central authority.
An individual pair's exchange rate cannot be centrally dictated or observed by a single coordinator: it is set locally across many separate interfaces.
The overall shape of who connects to whom does not match any simple pairing rule that either participant applies on its own; the pattern only emerges when all exchanges are taken together.
New participants can attach to and draw from connections made earlier by participants they have never interacted with directly, so membership in this web is open and accumulates over time.
excludes: A system that simply splits a single flow through two stations one after another, where the total passing through equals the original amount conserved — here there is no mutual giving to each other.
A pairing governed by fixed rules and shared records: matching by type or schedule with everything logged centrally, so exchange rates are set from above rather than at each contact point.
Two participants that depend on one another for survival yet fuse into a single continuing entity — neither stays distinct and reproducing as its own kind.
schema.name: Emergent mutual-connection web
roles: Participant A: keeps its identity; can supply something others value; changes how much it supplies in response to what it receives.
Participant B: keeps its identity; can supply something else values; changes how much it supplies in response to what it receives.
The network: the whole set of who-connects-to-whom, which forms a complex structure that no single participant encodes on its own.

conditions: There are two distinct kinds of participants that exchange a resource each holds in surplus for a resource the other holds in surplus.
Each participant can also operate without its partner, and actually does so from time to time (it is not permanently dependent).
Neither participant changes into or becomes part of the other; each keeps recognisable as what it was after an interaction. The change may be a reduction, but there must remain something continuous.

The two partners interact repeatedly over time and at many contact points rather than once. The relationship is distributed across these contacts rather than decided by one central authority or planner.
excludes: A single thing made of parts that cannot exist independently — the whole depends on each part to function, so there is no 'without partner' state.
A temporary transaction between strangers with no expectation of future exchange and nothing to carry it forward.
schema.name: Relational equilibrium
roles: A holder of a resource that the other needs
A provider of a resource that the first needs

conditions: The two roles exchange a resource each possesses and needs from the other: role A supplies what it can produce at low cost to itself; role B supplies what it cannot reach otherwise.
Each role receives exactly one counterflow of equal value, so neither keeps a surplus nor suffers a net loss (the flows balance by amount, not by matching parcels).
The relationship is bidirectional and mutually obligatory: both roles depend on the exchange for something they lack; dropping either role degrades or disables that partner.
Each role preserves its own identity while participating: it can still function as an independent unit when the link is broken, so neither becomes dependent only in form but also in substance.
excludes: Systems with unequal exchange where one party gains a net surplus at the other's expense (a dominant role that keeps more than it gives).
Hierarchical systems where influence or authority flows from top to bottom, rather than being distributed as an interdependent network.
Communal pooling without distinct roles: resources and burdens shared equally among interchangeable members with no specialisation.
schema.name: Symbiotic Exchange Structure
roles: A role that generates a resource (e.g., something it produces or fixes) but lacks access to another's resource.
B role that supplies a different resource (e.g., something it cannot reach alone) but depends on A for its own output.

conditions: Each role is identifiable by its position in a flow rather than by any intrinsic nature it carries.
The flow passes from one part to another and back; the parts are defined as the nodes where that exchange occurs, not as free-standing things that merely happen to be present.
There is no central authority or plan. The pattern of who connects to whom emerges from pairwise local decisions about what each side gives in return for what it gets.
The arrangement is maintained only while the connection exists; break the links and the structure relaxes back toward a form that did not require them.
Each part keeps its own independent capacity and reproductive path. Neither part becomes dependent on the other to persist or to multiply.
excludes: A system in which one part must convert, transform, or be absorbed into another (the joined parts stop being able to exist apart).
A system held together by a shared plan, schedule, or central decision-maker that assigns who connects with whom.
A loose coexistence of independent units that do not exchange anything and so have no pattern shaping which ones touch.
schema.name: Emergent Exchange Web
roles: Provider: the part that supplies one kind of resource along a flow.
Receiver: the part that takes that same resource in return for something it offers back.
Bridge: any intervening role whose position is defined only by where the two flows meet.

conditions: The relationship is fundamentally asymmetric: one part (the dependent) benefits from interaction with another part (the provider), while the other part's response to that benefit remains negligible for a sustained period.

There exists an initial window in which the recipient receives support or access without any detectable cost imposed on the source. The interaction must be non-reciprocal during this phase—not merely unequal, but directionally one-way.

The relationship is real and functional rather than incidental: it consistently produces a measurable effect (growth, acquisition, binding) in at least one system and remains quiescent or neutral in the other until some accumulated threshold of use is crossed.

There exists an identifiable tipping point where sustained use by the recipient eventually imposes load on the source. The transition from free to costly must be describable and checkable against the system's history.

The provider does not visibly change as a result of being used, at least within its own frame: it shows no awareness, retaliation, refusal, or adaptive response to the demand placed upon it, even though external observers may later note that its capacity has eroded.
excludes: Systems in which the dependency is mutual and continuous—the provider receives an equal and ongoing benefit from every exchange, so there is no one-way window. (Example of exclusion: a symbiosis where both parties depend on each other equally at all times.)

Relationships that are merely incidental or opportunistic—where contact happens to occur but produces no consistent functional effect in either system, because the interaction does not reliably yield anything usable.

Structures where the source demonstrably and immediately resists the demand—refusing outright, punishing the taker as soon as a threshold is passed, or withdrawing its support before any real benefit has been extracted. In such cases there is no sustained window of uncosted access to establish the pattern.
schema.name: asymmetric dependency with delayed cost
roles: the dependent: a component that gains something—access, support, binding capacity—by drawing on another system without initially paying for it
the provider: a component whose resources are drawn upon by the dependent and which does not reciprocate during the early phase of use

conditions: The relationship is directional: a signal flows one way from source to target and produces an effect on the target's state.
The target exists independently of the source; it does not require the source in order to exist or function as its own entity.
At typical operating levels, applying the source makes little or no measurable difference to the target; the relationship is effectively inert over a wide range.

When applied beyond that wide range—large enough quantity, intensity, duration, size, load, density, or strength—the source does alter the target's state in a graded way (the effect increases with how much of it there is).
The system can be described as having this structure without reference to any particular kind of substance, process, material, or entity.
No feedback loop carries an influence from the target back onto the source.
excludes: A relationship in which both participants depend on each other and neither can be defined apart from the other; such a pairing has no independent baseline state to perturb, so it cannot have an inert range.

A relationship that includes a return path of influence: if changes made by one party feed back to modify the other's behaviour or state, both parties are active participants rather than source and target.
schema.name: Perturbable baseline
roles: source (the thing supplied)
target (the thing affected)

conditions: A single primary actor exists (the 'resource-holder') that possesses an asset and is largely unaffected by its presence or absence.
An external agent extracts value from the asset without reciprocating anything in return for that extraction.

The interaction produces a persistent change to the resource-holder — either depletion of material, structural degradation, suppression of growth/output, or loss of integrity — such that it cannot fully recover over time.
There is an asymmetry between who bears the cost and who gains: one party loses, the other gains at no corresponding expense.
The system persists over repeated exchanges rather than as a single one-off transaction.
excludes: A relationship in which both parties receive reciprocal benefit for each contribution (e.g., mutual support where the scaffold also depends on and benefits from the climber).
An exchange with no net harm to either party, even if one side is more passive than the other.
Cooperation or cooperation-adjacent systems where costs are shared and returns are distributed among contributors.
schema.name: Asymmetric Extraction
roles: Resource-holder: possesses an asset (material, structural capacity, a binding site, a price level, or a lexical item) that can be drawn upon.
Extractor: gains value by consuming the holder's asset.

conditions: There are two role-classes in the system.
Each element of one class provides a resource to another element of the other class, and that provision is the primary reason the recipient depends on the provider.
The recipient can obtain its resource from many alternative providers within the same role-class; it does not require any particular individual provider.
excludes: Systems in which one side cannot substitute another partner for itself (i.e., the two parties are unique or irreplaceable, so the recipient depends on a specific individual rather than on its role).
Systems whose relationship is defined by an exclusive pairing or contract between designated individuals.
schema.name: Generic-Pool Dependency Structure
roles: Provider: possesses or generates a resource that others require.
Consumer: requires the resource and can draw on many alternative providers within its own role-class.

conditions: the source is consumed by its own act of supplying
there is no counter-action from the recipient
excludes: a system where both parts actively affect each other's state or growth
a system where the recipient strengthens itself in response to the source (e.g. by growing defenses)
a mutualistic arrangement where benefits flow in both directions over time
schema.name: asymmetric drain
roles: one part exists solely as a medium for another to act upon or pass through
another part depends on that medium and is shaped by drawing it down
the recipient leaves the source's form and dynamics unchanged
